Thirty Pieces of Silver
THUR-tee PEE-suhz uhv SIL-ver
noun (biblical sum)
From the Old English thritig, thirty, and seolfor, silver; the betrayal price paid to Judas Iscariot, rendering the Greek triakonta argyria.

Biblical Definition

The thirty pieces of silver were the price for which Judas Iscariot betrayed the Lord of glory, the wages he bargained from the chief priests: "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Matt 26:15). This sum was no arbitrary figure but the appointed price of a gored bondservant under the law: "If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver" (Exod 21:32). Thus the Son of God was valued at the price of a slave. When remorse seized Judas, he cast the silver into the temple and went and hanged himself; the priests, scrupling to put blood money into the treasury, bought the potter's field to bury strangers (Matt 27:3-10). In all this the ancient word of Zechariah was sovereignly fulfilled: "So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver" (Zech 11:12-13). This dictionary confesses that even the treachery of Judas and the greed of the priests served the unchangeable counsel of God, who ordained that His Son should be sold, that sinners might be bought back at the infinite price of His blood.

Webster 1828 Definition

The thirty pieces of silver were the sum for which Judas betrayed Christ, the legal price of a gored slave under Exodus 21:32. The money bought the potter's field. The transaction fulfilled Zechariah 11:12-13 to the letter.

THIRTY PIECES OF SILVER, noun. The sum of money for which Judas Iscariot betrayed the Lord Jesus to the chief priests.

It was the legal valuation of a slave gored by an ox under the Mosaic law (Exod 21:32), so that Christ was priced as a bondman.

"And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Matt 26:15).

It signifies the contempt of men for the Son of God, and the deceitfulness of covetousness in the heart of the traitor.

Its issue: the blood money bought the potter's field, and the prophecy of Zechariah was exactly fulfilled.

Key Scripture

Matt 26:15 — "And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver."

Exod 21:32 — "If the ox shall push a manservant or a maidservant; he shall give unto their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned."

Zech 11:12 — "And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver."

Matt 27:3 — "Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition, though critical scholarship treats the careful citation of Zechariah and Jeremiah as a clumsy invention rather than the sovereign fulfilment of prophecy.

expand to see more

The critical academy stumbles over Matthew's attribution of the potter's-field prophecy to Jeremiah while the words echo Zechariah, calling it a mistake or a fabricated proof-text. But the believing reader sees Matthew weaving together the strands of both prophets — Jeremiah's potter and field of blood (Jer 18-19, 32) and Zechariah's thirty pieces — under the inspiration of the Spirit, who is the true author of all Scripture and may cite His own word as He pleases.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the dreadful estimate that the world placed upon the Saviour: the price of a slave, weighed out in coin, for Him whom the heavens cannot contain. Let the redeemed weigh against it the precious blood by which they were bought, "not with corruptible things, as silver and gold" (1 Pet 1:18), and learn how cheaply the world reckons Christ and how dearly the Father loves His own.

Hebrew Roots

The phrase translates the Greek triakonta argyria, thirty silver coins, rooted in the Hebrew sheloshim keseph, the slave-price of Exodus 21:32.

expand to see more

The number thirty (Hebrew sheloshim) is fixed by the law as the redemption price of a gored servant (Exod 21:32).

The "piece of silver" here is the shekel, the standard weight of temple currency.

Greek argyria (silver coins) appears in Matthew's narrative of the betrayal and the priests' remorse.

Zechariah 11:12-13 supplies the prophetic pattern, the despised price cast to the potter in the house of the LORD.

Thus the phrase joins law, prophecy, and gospel in one appointed sum.

Usage

"For thirty pieces of silver Judas sold the Friend who had washed his feet."

"The thirty pieces of silver fulfilled to the letter what Zechariah had foretold of the despised Shepherd."

"The priests would not defile the treasury with the thirty pieces of silver, yet defiled their souls with innocent blood."
